questions.q: Define the PEEL structure for literature answers and state what each letter stands for.
questions.a: PEEL = Point (topic sentence stating your argument), Evidence (brief textual quote or reference), Explanation (analysis of how evidence supports point), Link (connect back to question/theme). A wrong answer (e.g., "Point, Example, Explain, Conclusion") reveals confusion with generic essay structures — PEEL is specific to literary analysis and requires the Link to tie back to the question's key terms.

questions.q: Explain in your own words why plot summary earns low marks in CBSE Class 12 literature answers, using "Tomorrow" as an example.
questions.a: Plot summary merely retells *what happens* (Hagberd waits, Harry returns, leaves) without analyzing *how the writer achieves effect*. Board marking schemes allocate marks for "analysis of literary devices," "interpretation," and "critical appreciation" — none for narration. A student who writes "Hagberd dug the garden every day waiting for his son" gets 1/6; one who writes "The daily digging ritual symbolizes Hagberd's futile attempt to control time, reinforced by the repetitive 'tomorrow' motif" gets 5/6.

questions.q: Apply PEEL to answer: "How does the fence between the cottages function as a symbol in 'Tomorrow'?" Write one complete PEEL paragraph.
questions.a: **Point:** The shared fence symbolizes the fragile boundary between Hagberd's delusion and Bessie's reality. **Evidence:** "For all their intimacy... they had never talked without a fence or a railing between them" (p.50). **Explanation:** The physical barrier mirrors emotional distance — Hagberd controls the interaction, inviting Bessie into his fantasy only on his terms (winks, patronizing talk), while she remains trapped in her dutiful role. **Link:** Thus the fence embodies the story's central tension: connection vs. isolation, appearance vs. truth. A wrong answer would describe the fence literally ("it separates gardens") without symbolic interpretation.

questions.q: Analyze how Conrad uses the character of Bessie Carvil as a foil to Captain Hagberd. Identify two contrasting traits with evidence.
questions.a: **Trait 1 — Agency vs. Delusion:** Bessie acts from necessity (nurses father, pays rent, manages household); Hagberd acts from fantasy (digs garden for imaginary homecoming). Evidence: Bessie "dragging with her for a penance the burden of that infirm bulk" (p.48) vs. Hagberd "turned it over and over several times every year, but was not going to plant anything 'just at present'" (p.44). **Trait 2 — Grounded empathy vs. Self-absorbed madness:** Bessie feels "vaguest pity" then "incredulous emotion" (p.44-45); Hagberd feels only "horror and incredulity" when his delusion is threatened (p.46). A weak answer lists traits without textual evidence or fails to explain *how* the contrast illuminates theme.

questions.q: Evaluate this student claim: "Harry Hagberd is the villain of the story because he exploits his father and Bessie." Defend or refute using textual evidence.
questions.a: Refute. Harry is morally ambiguous, not villainous. Evidence: He admits "I spent my last shillings on the railway fare" (p.61) — he's destitute, not greedy. His "five quid" motive (p.62) is survival, not malice. Conrad portrays him as a "Gambusino" — rootless, restless, shaped by his father's brutality ("chasing me upstairs with a hard leather strap," p.59). The true tragedy is systemic: Hagberd's madness created the son he rejects. A "villain" reading ignores Conrad's modernist complexity — no character is purely good/evil. Wrong answers treat characters as moral types rather than psychological portraits.

questions.q: Create an alternative ending for "Tomorrow" (50-60 words) where Bessie confronts Hagberd with the truth. Maintain Conrad's tone and character voices.
questions.a: Sample: "Bessie stood at the railing, spine straight. 'Captain, Harry came. He took my half-sovereign. He left.' Hagberd's spade clattered. 'Tomorrow—' he began. 'There is no tomorrow,' she said. 'Only today. And he's gone.' The sea-wall swallowed the silence." Good answers use Conrad's syntactic rhythm (short sentences, dashes), retain Hagberd's "tomorrow" fixation, show Bessie's new agency. Poor answers write modern dialogue or change character voices.
